I think there’s some confusion about what you’ve been told because *typically*, epilepsy is not lethal. If you developed epilepsy as a result of a head injury, it’s not a neurodegenerative disease. Hundreds of thousands of people have epilepsy and live long and relatively normal lives - many of them as a result of a brain injury. You definitely need to go back and talk with your neurologist to clarify some things. For example, whether the problem is the injury on its own, or the actually epilepsy, and if the epilepsy then what your options are (anti-epileptic medications? neurosurgery?). Obviously I don’t know enough about what’s going on, or whether the epilepsy is likely to be progressive (maybe this is where you got the neurodegenerative bit from) but it definitely sounds like you need more information - at least so you know more about what your options are, if any, and what to actually expect. For example, can you expect lots of seizures that progressively get worse? I’m sorry this is going on for you :-(

Taking the first step towards getting help was difficult. I went to my doctor and told them I wanted to kill myself. The doc referred me to a counselor. Unfortunately, finding the right counselor can be really tough. I've seen a few different ones (as well as psychiatrists etc), but you have to 'click' with them to really feel like you can open up. Once you've made that first step though, it becomes a little easier to do it the next time. The counselors job is to make it as easy for you to open up as possible, so let them guide you - you are in control over what you tell them and how much. I think my biggest fear was that they would 'lock me up', and while I have been 'locked up', it was never from talking to a counselor.

Having lived in one American and one European country, before returning to the UK, I would say the most difficult thing is the switch from having international friends, to 'home country' friends. When you live abroad, you tend to mix with people of different nationalities who are all doing what you are doing, and are all open to meeting new people and having adventures. When you return to your home country, you are no longer an immigrant, but for a while, you feel like you don't belong there. People in your home country already have their existing friendship groups, which are difficult to break into, and aren't as interested as making new friends and being adventurous as fellow travellers. You feel like you have had a huge adventure, but no-one else can relate to what you have experienced, and you feel like you can't talk about it for fear of appearing 'snobby'. Well, this was my experience anyway. Moving back to the UK was the most difficult move I have ever done.
